title: The Singalila Ridge: Border, Poison Hill and Land Rovers
meta_description: The Singalila Ridge story: the 1816 Nepal border, Hooker's rhododendrons, Sandakphu's poison name, the 1882 forest, the national park and the Land Rovers.
summary: The Singalila Ridge has been a frontier since the Anglo-Nepalese war of 1814–16, a reserve forest since the British bought it from Sikkim in 1882, and a national park since 1992. Botanists, mountaineers and herders crossed it long before trekkers did, and since the 1950s Maneybhanjan's Land Rovers have carried everyone up its stone track.

sections.heading: A ridge that became a border
paras: The Singalila Ridge runs north to south from the snows of Kanchenjunga down to Maneybhanjan, a long spur of rock and forest that splits the rivers of Nepal from those of Darjeeling and Sikkim. Rain falling on its west side runs into Nepal's Ilam district; rain on its east side feeds the Rammam, the Sri Khola and, in the end, the Teesta. A line that divides water so cleanly is an easy line to draw on a treaty map.

That is roughly what happened. In the late 1700s the Gorkha kingdom of Nepal pushed east into Sikkim, occupying much of the land that is now the Darjeeling hills. The British East India Company fought Nepal in the Anglo-Nepalese war of 1814–16, and the Treaty of Sugauli in 1816, followed by the Treaty of Titalia with Sikkim in 1817, pushed Nepal back to the west and returned the hills to the Sikkim ruler. Along this stretch the frontier settled on the crest of the ridge, which is why the trail today steps in and out of Nepal at Tumling, Jaubari and Kalipokhri.

sections.heading: Hooker on Tonglo
paras: In 1835 the Chogyal of Sikkim granted the British the hill of Darjeeling as a sanatorium, and within a few years the new town was looking west at the dark ridge on its skyline. In 1848 the young botanist Joseph Dalton Hooker, later director of Kew Gardens, arrived to collect plants of the Sikkim Himalaya. One of his first excursions was up 'Tonglo', the summit we now call Tonglu. His Himalayan Journals, published in 1854, describe forests dripping with moss, magnolias and rhododendrons in bewildering variety. Wikipedia's park article dates the visit to 1849; Hooker's journals point to 1848, and we follow the journals.

The seeds and descriptions Hooker sent home helped start the Victorian taste for Himalayan rhododendrons in British gardens. When you walk through the red tree rhododendrons above Chitrey in April, you are walking through the forest that, in a small way, changed the look of English country estates.

sections.heading: The height of the poisonous plant
paras: Sandakphu's name is usually traced to Lepcha and translated as 'the height of the poisonous plant'. The plant is aconite, Aconitum ferox, one of the most toxic plants known, which once grew thick on the upper slopes along with rhododendrons that sicken livestock. Herders driving sheep and cattle along the ridge are said to have muzzled their animals to cross it. A little south, the col of Bikheybhanjang carries the same warning in Nepali, where bikh means poison and bhanjyang means a pass.

For the British, the poison hill was the best place within reach of Darjeeling to see Everest. The Survey of India announced in 1856 that Peak XV was the highest mountain on earth, and by the later nineteenth century a ride up the ridge to Sandakphu and on to Phalut had become a classic Darjeeling excursion, done on ponies with porters carrying the baggage. In 1905 the Swiss doctor Jules Jacot-Guillarmod led the first documented attempt on Kanchenjunga, with the occultist Aleister Crowley in the party, and the expedition marched north along this same ridge toward the mountain's south-west face.

sections.heading: Bought forest, then a national park
paras: The slopes you walk through are still oak, rhododendron, magnolia and silver fir, not tea, because of a purchase made in 1882. That year the British government bought the Singalila tract from the Sikkim Durbar and notified it as reserve forest. Villages already on the ridge and its eastern flank kept farming, but felling and grazing came under forest rules that tightened over the following century.

In 1986 the forest became Singalila Wildlife Sanctuary, and in 1992 it was upgraded to Singalila National Park, covering about 78.6 square kilometres of the ridge and its upper slopes. The park protects one of the best red panda habitats in India, and the Padmaja Naidu Himalayan Zoological Park in Darjeeling has released captive-bred red pandas into its forests. The rule that every group must take a licensed local guide, and the monsoon closure from about mid-June to mid-September, both come from the park administration. The guide mandate and closure dates are revised from time to time, so check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: The Land Rovers of Maneybhanjan
paras: For most of the twentieth century there was no road up the ridge, only a mule and pony track. When a stone and cobble track was finally laid, roughly 31 km from Maneybhanjan to Sandakphu with gradients that defeat most cars, the vehicles that could manage it were the British-built Series Land Rovers of the 1950s and 1960s. Maneybhanjan kept them long after the rest of India moved on.

Today the town's Land Rover owners' association runs a fleet that sources put at around forty, many of them more than half a century old. Local mechanics keep them going with salvaged and hand-made parts. Each vehicle seats about six, works on a rota, and charges rates set by the association. The trekkers who ride up for the Everest view are only part of their work: the same Land Rovers carry rations, gas cylinders, building materials and schoolchildren for the ridge villages, and they are the only motor link for Nepal-side hamlets such as Tumling.

There are changes coming. The track has been widened and partly paved in places, and a motor road from the Nepal side now reaches the upper ridge. How these roads affect the Land Rover rota and the park's rules is still settling, so check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: People of the ridge today
paras: The families who run lodges and guide trekkers are mostly Nepali-speaking: Sherpa, Tamang, Gurung, Rai, Limbu and others whose grandparents farmed potatoes, kept cattle and traded along the ridge. Tumling's few households, many of them Gurung, are Nepali citizens who reach the outside world on an Indian track. Rimbik, at the eastern foot, grew as a market for roadless villages such as Gorkhey and Rammam, and its higher secondary school dates to 1948.

Since 2001 India's Sashastra Seema Bal has guarded the Nepal border, and its camps at Gairibas, Sandakphu and Phalut are part of the ridge now, along with prayer flags, chortens and the small gompas at Chitrey and Meghma. On a clear morning at Sandakphu, Indian soldiers, Nepali lodge owners, Bengali families and foreign backpackers stand in the same cold wind looking at the same mountains. That mix, more than any single date, is the ridge's story.

If you want to see this history rather than read it, look for it in small things on the walk: the culvert in Maneybhanjan bazaar that marks the border, the boundary pillars beside the trail above Tumling, the chorten at Chitrey, the SSB sentry at Sandakphu, the dark pond at Kalipokhri hung with flags, and a Land Rover older than your parents grinding past with gas cylinders on its roof.

faqs.q: What does the name Sandakphu mean?
faqs.a: It is usually traced to Lepcha and translated as 'the height of the poisonous plant'. The plant is aconite, Aconitum ferox, which once grew thickly on the upper slopes, along with rhododendrons harmful to livestock. Herders are said to have muzzled their animals to cross. The pass of Bikheybhanjang below carries the same idea in Nepali, from bikh, poison.

faqs.q: Why does the Sandakphu trail go in and out of Nepal?
faqs.a: Because the India–Nepal border follows the crest of the Singalila Ridge, a frontier settled after the Anglo-Nepalese war by the Treaties of Sugauli in 1816 and Titalia in 1817. The trail keeps to the crest, so hamlets such as Tumling, Jaubari and Kalipokhri sit on the Nepal side or straddle the line. Carry photo ID; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How old are the Land Rovers at Maneybhanjan?
faqs.a: Many are Series Land Rovers built in the 1950s and 1960s, kept running by local mechanics with salvaged and hand-made parts. They were among the few vehicles able to climb the steep cobbled track to Sandakphu, and Maneybhanjan kept them long after they disappeared elsewhere. The owners' association fleet is usually put at around forty vehicles.

faqs.q: When did Singalila become a national park?
faqs.a: Singalila was declared a wildlife sanctuary in 1986 and upgraded to a national park in 1992. It covers about 78.6 square kilometres of the ridge in Darjeeling district. The forest had already been protected as reserve forest since the British bought the tract from the Sikkim Durbar in 1882, which is why it is still oak, rhododendron and fir.

faqs.q: Who was the first outsider to write about the Singalila Ridge?
faqs.a: The best-known early account is by the botanist Joseph Dalton Hooker, who climbed Tonglu from Darjeeling in 1848 and described its moss forests and rhododendrons in his Himalayan Journals of 1854. Some sources date the visit to 1849. Earlier travellers and herders certainly crossed the ridge, but Hooker's is the account that made it known in Britain.

faqs.q: Did mountaineers use the Singalila Ridge to reach Kanchenjunga?
faqs.a: Yes. In 1905 the first documented attempt on Kanchenjunga, led by the Swiss doctor Jules Jacot-Guillarmod with Aleister Crowley in the party, marched north from Darjeeling along the Singalila Ridge toward the mountain's south-west face. The attempt failed after an avalanche killed several members of the party. The ridge was the obvious approach from the Darjeeling side.

faqs.q: Who guards the border on the Sandakphu trek?
faqs.a: On the Indian side, the Sashastra Seema Bal, which took over guarding the India–Nepal border in 2001, has camps at places such as Gairibas, Sandakphu and Phalut. Nepal police and armed police may be present on the Nepal side. Both may check papers, so Indians should carry a passport or voter ID and foreigners a passport with visa. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Who lives on the Singalila Ridge?
faqs.a: Mostly Nepali-speaking families of Sherpa, Tamang, Gurung, Rai, Limbu and other communities, who farm potatoes and keep cattle and now run lodges and guide trekkers. Some ridge hamlets, such as Tumling, are in Nepal's Ilam district. The eastern villages, including Gorkhey, Rammam, Srikhola and Rimbik, are in Darjeeling district.

faqs.q: Is there a road to Sandakphu now?
faqs.a: Yes. A steep cobbled track of about 31 km runs from Maneybhanjan to Sandakphu, used mainly by the town's Land Rovers, and parts have been widened and paved. A motor road from the Nepal side also reaches the upper ridge. Rules on which vehicles may use which stretch change, so check current status before you travel.
